items.title: postcbor
items.text:
postcbor is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a cbor type: the CBOR counterpart of jsonb. Values are stored in one canonical binary form, with the operators, functions and indexes you know from jsonb, extended to everything CBOR can hold: byte strings, tags, map keys of any type, exact integers of any size, floats kept apart from integers, undefined and simple values.

Built with AI

postcbor was written entirely by an AI model, Claude, directed by a human. See How this was built before you rely on it.

CREATE EXTENSION postcbor;

SELECT '{"name": "ann", 1: h''cafe'', "when": 1(1700000000), "n": 2.5}'::cbor;
-- {1: h'cafe', "n": 2.5, "name": "ann", "when": 1(1700000000)}

SELECT '{"name": "ann", 1: h''cafe''}'::cbor -> 1;
-- h'cafe'

items.title: When to use it
items.text:
• Your application already speaks CBOR. JavaScript applications using cbor-x can send their request bodies straight to a cbor column: cbor-x records and packing are unpacked on input, and cbor_pack gives them back in cbor-x's form.
  • CWT and COSE tokens. Their claims maps use integer keys and byte strings; cwt -> 1 reads key 1 directly.
  • Device and telemetry payloads, which are often CBOR already, with tags for dates and binary fields.
  • Exact data. Integers beyond 64 bits stay exact, 1 and 1.0 stay distinct, bytes stay bytes. Small values also take less space than in jsonb.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• Install it.
  • Coming from jsonb lists the differences that might surprise you.
  • Text form shows how to write values in SQL.
  • Operators, Functions, Path queries and Indexes are the reference.

postcbor supports PostgreSQL 15 to 18, on UTF-8 databases only.

items.title: CBOR bytes
items.text:
bytea::cbor (or cbor_from_bytea) decodes CBOR bytes; cbor::bytea gives the canonical encoding. The binary protocol (COPY … BINARY, binary parameters and results) uses the same canonical encoding.

SELECT '\xa2616101616202'::bytea::cbor;
-- {"a": 1, "b": 2}

SELECT '{"a": 1}'::cbor::bytea;
-- \xa1616101

Bytes go through the same checks and the same normalization as text input. Input must be a single CBOR item: a CBOR sequence (several items back to back) is refused.

items.title: Packed CBOR
items.text:
Packed CBOR shares repeated items (strings, map shapes) through tables and references, so the bytes are smaller. postcbor unpacks it on every input path: what is stored, compared and indexed is always the plain value.

Recognized on input:

  • cbor-x records, cbor-x's default for arrays of similar objects (tags 57342, 57343, 57344 and above).
  • cbor-x packing (cbor-x's pack option, tag 51).
  • IETF Packed CBOR (draft-ietf-cbor-packed-19): table setup tags 113 and 1113, shared item and argument references, and the join and record functions (tags 105, 106, 114).

Refused:

  • cbor-x shared or sequential structures, whose definitions live outside the value (in the encoder or a previous message): a reference to a structure not defined earlier in the same value is an error.
  • cbor-x bundleStrings, which writes strings after the value, so the input is not a single item.
  • IETF tables supplied by the application rather than in the value.

Outside a table setup tag, the reference tags and simple values 0–15 are ordinary values and are kept as written.

cbor_pack(value, format) gives packed bytes, 'cbor-x' (the default) or 'ietf'. The same value always packs to the same bytes.

SELECT encode(cbor_pack('[{"name": "ann", "age": 30}, {"name": "bob", "age": 41}]', 'cbor-x'), 'hex');
-- 82d9dfff8419e0008263616765646e616d65181e63616e6ed9e00082182963626f62

SELECT cbor_pack('[{"name": "ann", "age": 30}, {"name": "bob", "age": 41}]', 'cbor-x')::cbor;
-- [{"age": 30, "name": "ann"}, {"age": 41, "name": "bob"}]

'cbor-x' turns maps with a repeated set of text keys into records. 'ietf' puts text and byte strings of 3 bytes or more that appear at least twice into a tag 113 table. A value holding plain simple values 0–15 or tags 6 or 128–143 is returned unpacked in 'ietf' format, since inside tag 113 they would read as references.

Compatibility with cbor-x is tested against cbor-x 1.6.7: its records and pack output read back as the plain value, and cbor_pack(…, 'cbor-x') decodes in cbor-x to the original objects.

items.title: Limits
items.text: Packed input can unpack to far more than its own size. Input is refused when the unpacked value is more than postcbor.max_expansion_ratio times the input (default 16) or larger than postcbor.max_expanded_size (default 256MB); see Settings and limits.

items.title: Casts and JSON
items.text: All casts are explicit: write value::int8, value::jsonb and so on.

items.title: From cbor
To json and jsonb
items.text:
JSON cannot represent everything CBOR can. ::jsonb and ::json follow the conversion advice of RFC 8949, section 6.1:

CBOR JSON byte strings base64url text, without padding keys that are not text their EDN text NaN, infinities null undefined null bignums, decimal fractions, bigfloats numbers, when numeric can hold them other tags their content (the tag is dropped) simple values other than true, false, null null 
SELECT '{"b": h''ff'', 1: 2, "n": NaN, "t": 1(5), "d": 4([-2, 12345])}'::cbor::jsonb;
-- {"1": 2, "b": "_w", "d": 123.45, "n": null, "t": 5}

cbor_to_jsonb_strict(value) converts the same way but raises an error instead of losing information:

SELECT cbor_to_jsonb_strict('{"b": h''ff''}');
-- ERROR:  byte strings have no JSON form

items.title: From json and jsonb
items.text:
jsonb::cbor and json::cbor keep the structure. Integers become CBOR integers (bignums when they need more than 64 bits); other numbers become the nearest 64-bit float.

SELECT '{"a": 1, "b": 1.5, "c": 123456789012345678901234567890}'::jsonb::cbor;
-- {"a": 1, "b": 1.5, "c": 2(h'018ee90ff6c373e0ee4e3f0ad2')}

jsonb keeps 1.0 as written, so it becomes the float 1.0, not the integer 1.

items.title: to_cbor
items.text:
to_cbor(anyelement) converts any SQL value, as to_jsonb does:

SQL type CBOR bool true, false int2, int4, int8 integer float4, float8 float numeric integer when whole (a bignum beyond 64 bits), otherwise a decimal fraction (tag 4) keeping the scale; NaN and infinities become floats text, varchar, char text string bytea byte string timestamptz tag 1 with the seconds since 1970 as a float timestamp the same, reading the value as UTC date tag 100 with the days since 1970 uuid tag 37 with the 16 bytes arrays arrays, nested for multi-dimensional arrays composite types and records map with the column names as text keys json, jsonb as the cast above cbor the value itself domains as their base type anything else its text output, as a text string 
SELECT to_cbor(row(2.50::numeric, '\xff'::bytea, '2024-01-01'::date, ARRAY[[1, 2], [3, 4]]));
-- {"f1": 4([-2, 250]), "f2": h'ff', "f3": 100(19723), "f4": [[1, 2], [3, 4]]}

items.title: Coming from jsonb
items.text: cbor works like jsonb: same operators, cbor_* functions for every jsonb_* one, same index classes. These are the differences that might surprise you.

items.title: Integers and floats are different values
items.text:
jsonb stores every number as numeric, so 1 and 1.0 are equal. In CBOR they are different types, and cbor keeps them apart:

SELECT '1'::cbor = '1.0'::cbor, '{"a": 1}'::cbor @> '{"a": 1.0}';
-- f | f

Equality, containment, DISTINCT, btree, hash and GIN indexes are all typed. Path queries are the exception: inside a jsonpath, numbers compare by value, as SQL/JSON requires ('1'::cbor @@ '$ == 1.0' is true). Cast to numeric to compare numbers loosely in SQL.

Floats are binary: 0.1 is the nearest 64-bit float, not the exact decimal. For exact decimals, use numeric's conversion: to_cbor(0.1::numeric) gives the decimal fraction 4([-1, 1]).

items.title: Keys can be anything
items.text:
Map keys can be integers, byte strings, floats, tags, even arrays. The operators accept text, integer and byte-string keys:

SELECT v -> 'a', v -> 1, v -> '\x01'::bytea
FROM (SELECT '{"a": 1, 1: 2, h''01'': 3}'::cbor AS v) s;
-- 1 | 2 | 3

In jsonb, an integer on the right only indexes arrays; on a cbor map it reads that integer key. Text that looks like a number is still text: -> '1' reads the text key "1", not integer key 1.

For other keys, and for paths whose steps keep their type, use cbor_get, cbor_get_path and friends. A quoted literal passed to an overloaded function is read as text: write cbor_delete(v, '1'::cbor) to delete integer key 1.

cbor_each and cbor_object_keys return keys as cbor, not text, so their type survives.

items.title: ->> on non-strings gives EDN
items.text:
->> gives a text string's text, as in jsonb. Anything else comes back as its EDN text, so bytes show as h'…' and tags as 1(…):

SELECT '{"b": h''ff'', "t": 1(1700000000)}'::cbor ->> 'b';
-- h'ff'

items.title: Key order
items.text:
As in jsonb, keys are sorted rather than kept in insertion order. Text keys come in the same order as in jsonb (shorter first, then bytewise). Keys of other types sort by type: integers and byte strings before text, then arrays, maps, tags, and finally floats and simple values.

SELECT '{"b": 1, "a": 2, 10: 3}'::cbor;
-- {10: 3, "a": 2, "b": 1}

items.title: Text sorts by code point
items.text: jsonb sorts strings with the database collation; cbor sorts them by their UTF-8 bytes, which is code-point order. "B" < "a" in cbor, whatever the collation.

items.title: Converting to jsonb loses information
items.text: ::jsonb turns bytes into base64url text, non-text keys into their EDN text, NaN, infinities and undefined into null, and drops tags. Use cbor_to_jsonb_strict to get an error instead. See Casts.

items.title: More values exist
items.text: undefined and simple values have their own types and are not null. cbor_strip_nulls removes null only, unless you pass strip_undefined => true. cbor_typeof returns integer or float rather than number, and map rather than object.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
• core/: the pure Rust crate (postcbor-core) that does every byte-level operation: parsing, normalization, EDN, comparison, containment, packing, GIN entries, jsonpath evaluation. No dependencies and no unsafe code.
  • postcbor/: the pgrx extension that exposes the core to SQL: types, operators, functions, casts, settings, errors.
  • fuzz/: cargo-fuzz targets over the core.
  • docs/content/: this site. design.md is the specification.

In the repository, AGENTS.md holds the coding rules, CONTEXT.md the domain terms, docs/adr/ the recorded decisions and their reasons, and TODO.md the implementation plan.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
Command Runs make test core unit tests, then the SQL suites (postcbor/tests/pg_regress/) against pgrx's PostgreSQL of the same major version as PG_CONFIG make test-matrix the same on PostgreSQL 15, 16, 17 and 18 (register them once with cargo pgrx init) make clippy clippy with warnings as errors make miri the core tests under Miri (nightly toolchain) make fuzz each fuzz target for FUZZ_SECONDS (default 60; nightly toolchain) make crosscheck random values encoded by Python's cbor2, normalized by the core and compared make cborx-check CBORX_NODE_MODULES=… round trips through a real cbor-x installation

CI (GitHub Actions, .github/workflows/ci.yml) runs clippy and the SQL suites on each PostgreSQL version, Miri, and each fuzz target for 30 seconds.

New fuzz corpus entries and crash reproducers are committed as regression cases.

items.title: Docs
items.text:
make docs         # build into docs/site
make docs-serve   # serve with live reload

Both run a pinned version of Zensical through uvx, so only uv needs to be installed. The build is strict: a broken link fails it.

The published site is versioned: each release vX.Y.Z has its docs under X.Y/, latest/ points at the newest release (the default), and dev/ follows main. CI publishes them (.github/workflows/docs.yml) with make docs-deploy, which runs Zensical's fork of mike and commits each version to the gh-pages branch. A patch release replaces its X.Y docs.

items.title: postcbor design
items.text: This is the reference specification: how postcbor behaves, exactly. The user pages describe the same behaviour less formally. In the repository, CONTEXT.md defines the terms used here, docs/adr/ records the reasons behind decisions (cited as ADR-NNNN), and TODO.md tracks the implementation plan.

items.title: 1. Goals and scope
items.text:
• A cbor type that does for CBOR what jsonb does for JSON: the same operators, the same functions (named cbor_* instead of jsonb_*), and the same index support, extended to the full CBOR data model.
  • Extension name postcbor, type name cbor. Operator symbols are the same as jsonb's, plus ?#, ?#| and ?#& for keys of any type.
  • PostgreSQL 15–18.
  • Install with make && make install (a wrapper around cargo pgrx install). Pre-built packages are out of scope for now.

items.title: 2. Threat model and limits
items.text:
Input is untrusted. Bytes arrive from web applications over the internet through ::cbor, cbor_recv (binary protocol) and the bytea casts. Every input path goes through the same validation and normalization.

The stored datum is trusted after input, as with jsonb. Debug builds (debug_assertions) re-validate every datum they read, to catch format bugs.

Setting Default Context Applies to postcbor.max_depth 512 SUSET Nesting depth on every input path and in builders. Each array, map and tag counts as one level. postcbor.max_expansion_ratio 16 SUSET Body size after normalization divided by input size. Matters for packed input. postcbor.max_expanded_size 256MB (unit kB) SUSET Absolute body size after normalization.

The index section is not counted in the expansion limits. Results of edits (||, cbor_set, subscript assignment, …) are held to postcbor.max_depth too: || can wrap a value in an array, and a stored value deeper than input accepts could not be dumped and restored (found by fuzzing). Values are also limited to PostgreSQL's 1 GB varlena maximum.

Errors raised, by SQLSTATE:

Condition SQLSTATE Malformed CBOR, invalid EDN, invalid UTF-8, duplicate keys, invalid bignum 22P02 invalid_text_representation (22P03 invalid_binary_representation for cbor_recv) Depth or expansion limit exceeded 54000 program_limit_exceeded Cast out of range 22003 numeric_value_out_of_range Cast from the wrong CBOR type 22023 invalid_parameter_value Allocation failure on an input-sized buffer 53200 out_of_memory

items.title: 3. Data model and normalization
items.text:
Every accepted input is normalized into the deterministic encoding. Normalization rules, in addition to well-formedness:

  1. Shortest heads: integers, lengths, tag numbers and simple values use the shortest head encoding.
  2. Definite lengths only: indefinite-length arrays and maps become definite. Indefinite-length strings are joined into one definite string. Every chunk must be a definite string of the same major type.
  3. Floats: stored in the shortest of f16/f32/f64 that represents the value exactly, including subnormals. Any NaN (any sign, any payload) becomes f97e00. Infinity is f97c00, -Infinity is f9fc00, and -0.0 is f98000 (kept distinct from 0.0).
  4. Map keys: sorted by bytewise lexicographic order of their deterministic encodings (RFC 8949 core deterministic ordering). After key normalization, duplicate keys are an error. Example: {1: 0, 2(h'01'): 0} is rejected.
  5. Bignums (tags 2/3): the content must be a byte string. Leading zero bytes are stripped. A value that fits in 64 bits becomes a major type 0 or 1 integer. Tag 2: n ≤ 2⁶⁴−1. Tag 3: −1−n with n ≤ 2⁶⁴−1.
  6. Text strings must be valid UTF-8.
  7. Simple values 24–31, and the two-byte form f8 with a value below 32, are rejected (not well-formed). Every other simple value is kept.
  8. Other tags are kept as they are, with their content normalized like any other value. The packing tags listed in section 6 are not "other tags": rule 11 consumes them first. Interpreted tags other than 2/3 are not checked on input. Their content is validated when an operation interprets them, for example a cast to timestamptz.
  9. Byte strings, including tag 24 (embedded CBOR) and <<…>> output, are opaque. Their content is not normalized.
  10. Single item only: trailing bytes after the item are an error (CBOR sequences are not accepted). So are reserved additional-info values 28–30 and a break code outside an indefinite-length item.
  11. Packed input is unpacked (section 6).

Interpreted tags:

Tag Meaning Used by 0 RFC 3339 date-time text cast to timestamptz 1 epoch date-time (number) cast to timestamptz, to_cbor(timestamptz) 2, 3 bignum normalization, comparison, numeric casts 4 decimal fraction numeric casts 5 bigfloat numeric casts (exact: m × 2⁻ⁿ has n decimal places, up to numeric's 16383) 37 UUID (16-byte string) uuid casts 52, 54 IPv4 / IPv6 address or prefix EDN IP'' literal 100 days since epoch (RFC 8943) date casts, to_cbor(date)

items.title: 4. Datum format
items.text:
datum  = header body [index body_len]
header = 1 byte:
         bits 0-1  format version (0 = this format)
         bit  2    has_index
         bits 3-7  reserved, 0
body   = deterministic encoding of the value
index  = dir_count:u32
         dir_count × { container_offset:u32, table:u32 }
         tables: sampled entry offsets, u16 or u32 each, in directory order
body_len = u32 little-endian, the last 4 bytes of the datum, present only when has_index
  • body_len sits at the end, not after the header, so the body can be written straight into the output buffer before it is known whether an index section will follow. The header byte is written last, in place.
  • All integers in the index section are little-endian. They are read through the cursor (from_le_bytes on slices), so nothing needs alignment.
  • Indexed container: an array or map with at least INDEX_THRESHOLD (16) entries. Smaller containers are scanned directly.
  • Container directory: one entry per indexed container, sorted by container_offset (offset of the container's head from the start of the body), which is depth-first body order. table is the byte position of its entry table in the tables area; its top bit set means the table holds 2-byte offsets.
  • Entry table: the offset of every STRIDE-th (8th) entry: entries 0, 8, 16, …, so ⌈n / 8⌉ offsets for n entries. Each offset is relative to the container's start and points at an array element, or at a map key (its value follows the key). A table uses 2-byte offsets when all of them fit, 4-byte otherwise. Sampling and narrow offsets cut the index from 4 bytes to about 0.25 byte per entry, which lets large values compress (see the benchmark in TODO.md).
  • Lookups:
  • Array element i: read sample ⌊i / 8⌋, then step over i mod 8 elements.
  • Map key: binary search over the sampled keys (comparing the lookup key's deterministic encoding bytewise) for the last sample ≤ the key, then scan at most 8 entries from it.
  • Skipping a whole indexed container: jump to its last sample, then step over the rest.
  • To descend into a nested container: binary search the directory for its offset.
  • Extracting a sub-value at body range [s, e):
  • The directory entries with s ≤ container_offset < e form a contiguous run [a, b), and their tables are contiguous too.
  • The new datum is: a header, the body slice, then (if b > a) the directory run with container_offset − s and table positions moved down by the run's first table position (width flags kept), the table bytes, and body_len.
  • No entry table is rebuilt.
  • Building: the index is built in one walk over the finished body (also used for values built by edits). The same walk enforces postcbor.max_depth.
  • Detoasting: datums are read with pg_detoast_datum_packed (a 1-byte varlena header is fine, since we only read bytes).
  • Format version: any version other than 0 is rejected with an error asking the user to upgrade the extension.

items.title: Input (cbor_in, text::cbor)
items.text:
Accepted: - Whitespace and comments: # … to end of line, / … /. - Integers: decimal with optional sign, 0x/0o/0b prefixes. Any magnitude: values beyond 64 bits become bignums (tags 2/3). - Floats: decimal with . and/or an exponent; NaN, Infinity, -Infinity. - Encoding indicators: _0–_3 and _i after a number or a container or string opener, and _ for indefinite length ([_ …], {_ …}, (_ "a", "b")). They are parsed and ignored, since the value is normalized anyway. - Text: "text" with JSON escapes, including \u surrogate pairs. - Byte strings: - 'text': the UTF-8 bytes of the text. - h'…': hex, with whitespace and comments allowed inside. - b64'…': standard or URL-safe alphabet, padding optional. - <<item, …>>: the deterministic encodings of the items, concatenated. - Containers: [ … ] and { key: value, … }. A trailing comma is an error. - Tags: N(item). - Simple values: simple(n), true, false, null, undefined. - Application literals (draft-ietf-cbor-edn-literals-29):

Literal Result dt'…' RFC 3339 → epoch number: an integer, or a float when there is a fractional part DT'…' the same number wrapped in tag 1 ip'…' address → byte string; prefix (/n) → [n, trimmed bytes] IP'…' the same wrapped in tag 52 (IPv4) or tag 54 (IPv6)

Rejected with a syntax error naming the feature: b32''/h32'', string concatenation, ellipsis ..., raw strings, hex floats, other application literals.

items.title: Output (cbor_out, ->> on anything other than a text string)
items.text:
Core EDN only, written deterministically: - Separators: ", " between items and ": " after keys, as jsonb_out does. - Integers: decimal. - Bignums over 64 bits: 2(h'…') / 3(h'…'). - Floats: the shortest decimal that reads back as the same value. It always contains . or e (1.0, 1.5e300). Special values print as NaN, Infinity, -Infinity, -0.0. - Text: JSON escaping; other characters are written as they are (databases are UTF-8, ADR-0010). - Bytes: h'…' in lowercase hex. - Tags: N(item). - Simple values: simple(n), true, false, null, undefined.

cbor_diag(c, pretty => true) and cbor_pretty(c) indent with 4 spaces, one entry per line, like jsonb_pretty.

Only UTF-8 databases are supported: CREATE EXTENSION refuses others (ADR-0010).

items.title: 6. Packed input
items.text:
Unpacking happens during normalization, on every input path (cbor_in, cbor_recv, bytea::cbor, cbor_from_bytea). There is no opt-out: stored data never contains packing (ADR-0005).

Idempotence (required): normalizing a stored body again gives exactly the same body. If unpacking could be turned off, a stored packing tag would be unpacked on restore (pg_dump goes through cbor_out/cbor_in or send/recv), and the value would change. This is why there is no opt-out.

Packing schemes recognized: - IETF Packed CBOR (draft-ietf-cbor-packed-19): - Table setup tags 113 and 1113. - Inside their scope: shared item references (simple values 0–15, tag 6 with an integer), argument references (tags 128–143, tag 6 with an array), and function tags 105 (ijoin), 106 (join) and 114 (record). - Outside any table setup tag: simple values 0–15 are plain simple values, and tags 6, 105, 106, 114 and 128–143 are plain tags. Tables supplied by the application environment (for example a media type) are not supported. - cbor-x records (cbor-records spec; the tags the current cbor-x encoder emits): - 57342: record definitions - 57343: inline record - 57344–65535 (0xe000 + id): record references, unpacked to maps with text keys. cbor-x reads every tag from 0xe000 as a reference (8192 ids), wider than the cbor-records spec's 57344–57599.

A reference to a structure not defined earlier in the same value is an error. This covers cbor-x shared and sequential structures, which are kept outside the data. cbor-x's legacy inline-record tag 105 is not supported: it clashes with IETF ijoin. - cbor-x's own packing (pack option): an older packed-CBOR draft, using tag 51 for the table, with tag 6 and simple-value references inside its scope. - cbor-x bundled strings (bundleStrings): not supported. cbor-x writes the strings after the value, so the input is not a single item and is refused.

Limits: expansion is bounded by postcbor.max_expansion_ratio and postcbor.max_expanded_size, nesting by postcbor.max_depth. A reference cycle is an error.

Implementation (core/src/pack.rs): - Normalization stops with an internal signal when it meets a table-setup or record tag (113, 1113, 51, 57342–65535); only then is the input decoded into an arena and resolved. Unpacked input pays nothing. - Resolution uses an explicit task stack and per-tag scopes: new table entries use the new number space, inherited ones keep theirs (draft §3). - Argument references combine argument and rump per draft §2.3–2.4: arrays concatenate, maps merge (right wins, undefined removes), strings concatenate taking the rump's string type, string with array joins. Function tags 105 (ijoin), 106 (join) and 114 (record) apply when the left-hand side is such a tag. - cbor-x tag 51 is [values, prefixes, suffixes, rump]; only the value table is used (cbor-x's encoder writes empty prefix and suffix tables). - Reference chains longer than 64 are rejected (loops); every arena node is charged against a memory budget of four times the output limit. - Output packing is deterministic: ietf puts strings of 3+ bytes used at least twice into a tag 113 table (largest saving first, ties by bytes), except when the value holds plain simple values 0–15 or tags 6/128–143, which would read as references inside tag 113 (found by fuzzing): such values are returned unpacked; cbor-x turns maps whose text-key set repeats into an inline record definition (57343) at first use and record references (57344+) afterwards, up to 8191 structures (ids up to 0xfffe; cbor-x confuses id 8191 with its inline-definition tag). - A value packed more than postcbor.max_expansion_ratio times smaller than its unpacked form is rejected on input; raise the setting for such data.

Output: cbor_pack(c cbor, format text DEFAULT 'cbor-x') → bytea. - 'cbor-x' emits records (57342/57344+). - 'ietf' emits tag 113. - The packer must be deterministic: the same value always gives the same bytes.

items.title: 7. Comparison, equality, hashing
items.text:
• Equality is byte equality of bodies. The header and index section are never compared.
  • Hashing works on the body bytes: hash_bytes / hash_bytes_extended with a seed.
  • Ordering (btree support function 1) must satisfy cmp(a, b) = 0 ⟺ body(a) = body(b). First by type rank:
  • numbers: unsigned and negative integers, floats, bignums (tags 2/3)
  • byte strings
  • text strings
  • arrays
  • maps
  • other tags
  • unassigned simple values
  • false
  • true
  • null
  • undefined
  • Within a rank:
  • Numbers: compared by exact mathematical value. Integers and floats are compared exactly, without going through f64. NaN sorts after every other number. When values are equal: integer < float, and -0.0 < 0.0.
  • Byte and text strings: bytewise lexicographic; a prefix sorts first. Text is compared as UTF-8 bytes, with no collation (ADR-0007).
  • Arrays: element by element; a prefix sorts first.
  • Maps: fewer entries sort first. Then key 1, value 1, key 2, … in stored order.
  • Tags: by tag number, then by content.
  • Simple values: by number.

The property tests in section 10 check antisymmetry, transitivity, and agreement with byte equality and hashing.

items.title: Type and I/O
items.text: cbor (varlena, storage extended), with: - cbor_in / cbor_out: EDN. - cbor_recv / cbor_send: the deterministic CBOR body. recv goes through full validation and normalization.

items.title: Operators
items.text:
Operator Right operand Result Notes -> int cbor Array index (negative counts from the end), or integer key on a map -> text, bytea cbor Text key, byte-string key ->> same as -> text Text string → its text; null → SQL NULL; anything else → EDN #> / #>> text[] cbor / text Text path, jsonb rules @>, <@ cbor bool Containment, jsonb semantics. Out-of-range indexes and missing keys return NULL, as in jsonb.

Why keys of any type and typed paths are not operators. Tested on PG 18: once an operator (cbor, cbor) exists, an untyped literal on the right is read as cbor. doc -> 'a' then fails as invalid EDN, and doc -> '1' silently looks up integer key 1. PostgreSQL first tries the left operand's type for an unknown literal. A separate key type does not help for paths either: #> '{a}' with both text[] and another type on the right is rejected as "operator is not unique". Only types that an untyped literal never resolves to are overloaded on operators (int, bytea, text, text[]). Keys of any type and typed paths go through functions with their own names (below). The existence checks also get operators with their own symbols, ?#, ?#| and ?#&, so that GIN indexes can serve them: a symbol with a single (cbor, cbor) definition captures no other operator's literals.

Typed-key functions:

Function Equivalent cbor_get(doc, key cbor), cbor_get_text(doc, key cbor) -> / ->> with a key of any type, or an array index cbor_get_path(doc, path cbor), cbor_get_path_text(doc, path cbor) #> / #>> with a typed path cbor_has(doc, key cbor), cbor_has_any(doc, keys cbor), cbor_has_all(doc, keys cbor) ?, ?|, ?& with keys of any type (keys is a CBOR array) cbor_delete(doc, key cbor), cbor_delete_path(doc, path cbor) -, #- cbor_set_path, cbor_set_lax_path, cbor_insert_path cbor_set, cbor_set_lax, cbor_insert with a typed path

These use different names rather than overloads because function overloads (cbor, text[]) and (cbor, cbor) are equally ambiguous for an untyped literal.

Selectivity estimators: matchingsel/matchingjoinsel for @> <@ ? ?| ?& ?# ?#| ?#&; eqsel/scalarltsel etc. for comparisons.

Operator classes: btree cbor_ops (default) and hash cbor_ops (default, with an extended hash function), and the GIN classes below.

items.title: GIN indexes
items.text:
Two operator classes, as for jsonb. Both are lossy: every match is rechecked against the row.

Class Operators Entries Storage cbor_ops (default) @> ? ?| ?& ?# ?#| ?#& @? @@ One per map key and one per atomic item, without their position, plus the path-equality form of items that differ from it bytea cbor_path_ops @> One per atomic item: a hash of the path leading to it and of the item int4

Both come from one walk over the value (core gin), in body order: - Atomic item: one that containment compares whole: a scalar, a tag whose content (through further tags) is atomic, or a decimal fraction or bigfloat (tags 4, 5). Arrays, maps and other tags around them are walked into. - cbor_ops entry: a role byte, then the item's deterministic encoding. Role 1 (key) for map keys, of any type and whole, and for array elements and the top-level value; role 2 for map values. Sharing the key role lets ? find array elements, as jsonb does. An item whose encoding is 125 bytes or longer gets instead the role with bit 7 set and a 4-byte hash of the encoding. - cbor_path_ops entry: a 32-bit hash over the path steps and the item: each map key's encoding and each walked tag's number, with a marker byte per step kind. Arrays add no step, since array containment ignores positions; so [1, 2] @> 1 holds for the index too. The hash is FNV-1a with a final mix. - Path-equality entry (cbor_ops only): for an atomic item whose jsonpath equality form differs from its encoding, a second entry with the same role holding that form: transparent tags removed, numbers in one form (an integer when whole, else a decimal fraction without trailing zeros), so 1, 1.0 and 4([-1, 10]) share one. Items a path literal cannot equal (byte strings, undefined, simple values, datetimes, NaN, numbers without a numeric value) have none. Plain integers and untagged strings add nothing. - Entries are on disk: changing the walk, the roles, the equality form or the hashes requires a REINDEX. cbor_ops indexes built before path-equality entries existed must be rebuilt.

Queries: - @>: the query value's own entries; the row must have all of them. A query with no entries ({}, [], {"a": {}}) scans the whole index and rechecks every row. - ?, ?|, ?&: the key-role entry of each text key. ?& with no keys matches every row; ?| with none matches no row. - ?#, ?#|, ?#&: the key-role entry of each key. A key that is not atomic cannot be found among array elements through entries, so ?# with such a key, or ?#| with any such key, rechecks every row; ?#& skips such keys. - @?, @@ (cbor_ops): as jsonb, from each accessors == literal condition (accessors: .key, .*, .**, […], [*], and filters on them): the key entries of its .key steps AND the literal's path-equality entry. The literal's role is the value role after a key step in strict mode, the key role after […] or at the top, and either one in lax mode or after .**. &&, || and ! combine conditions (NOT through De Morgan; ! of an equality gives nothing); an AND keeps the side that has entries. A path with no such condition scans the whole index. cbor_path_ops has no path support: its hashes include tags, which paths look through. - Strategy numbers: 7 @>, 9 ?, 10 ?|, 11 ?&, 15 @?, 16 @@ (jsonb's), 12 ?#, 13 ?#|, 14 ?#&.

items.title: Path queries
items.text:
@?, @@ and cbor_path_exists, cbor_path_match, cbor_path_query (set-returning), cbor_path_query_array, cbor_path_query_first, each with vars cbor (a map) and silent bool, plus the _tz variants. The path argument is PostgreSQL's jsonpath (ADR-0008). Results must equal jsonb's for every value that converts to jsonb without loss: the reference is jsonb_path_*(value::jsonb, …).

  • Compiled path: the jsonpath value's binary form is decoded in the core (format version 1, stable since PG 12; PG 17 appended the .bigint() … .timestamp_tz() items). Unknown versions and items are refused, and so are paths nesting deeper than 256 items (arguments and chained steps both count). The scalar functions and the operators keep the decoded path per call site; cbor_path_query, whose call site holds its set-returning state, decodes once per call.
  • Numbers: inside path expressions, numbers compare by value, as in SQL/JSON: 1 == 1.0, and bignums, decimal fractions and bigfloats are numbers. A float takes the value of its shortest decimal form, as when it is converted to jsonb. A number without a numeric value (a decimal fraction beyond numeric's range, a bigfloat with more than 16383 binary places) compares as unknown and is not a number for arithmetic. Containment and = stay typed.
  • CBOR types jsonpath lacks:
  • Byte strings: .type() is "bytes"; two byte strings compare by their bytes, and comparing them with other types is unknown, as jsonpath does for mismatched types.
  • Tags 2 and 3 are numbers, and tags 4 and 5 when their content is [integer, integer or bignum]; tags 0 and 1 are datetimes when their content is one (below); other tags are transparent (the path sees their content, and a result taken from the document keeps its tag).
  • Map keys that are not text: .key matches only text keys; .* and .keyvalue() visit every entry, and .keyvalue() gives the key as its CBOR value.
  • undefined and simple values keep their own types (.type() is "undefined", "simple"), unequal to null; simple values compare by number.
  • Arithmetic is decimal, as in SQL/JSON, and runs PostgreSQL's numeric functions, so results and scales match jsonb's. A result of scale 0 becomes an integer (a bignum if large); any other a decimal fraction (tag 4) keeping its scale: 2 * 3 is 6, 2 * 2.5 is 5.0, 4([-1, 50]). Results returned unchanged from the document keep their CBOR form (a float stays a float).
  • NaN and ±Infinity floats are numbers, ordered as numeric orders them: NaN equals itself and sorts above everything.
  • .keyvalue() ids are unique per object, as in jsonb, and equal to jsonb's for objects at the top of the document. jsonb derives the others from its own byte layout; ours come from positions in the CBOR value, so they differ.
  • Regex and datetimes: like_regex runs PostgreSQL's regex engine; the datetime methods use PostgreSQL's datetime parsing, casts and time zone rules (the _tz functions allow the casts that depend on the session time zone). A datetime result comes back as ISO 8601 text, as jsonb returns it. Tag 0 is a timestamptz when its text is RFC 3339 (shown with its own offset), tag 1 when its number of seconds is within timestamptz's range; otherwise the tag is transparent.
  • GIN: @? and @@ use cbor_ops for accessors == literal conditions (GIN indexes above); cbor_path_ops does not support them.

items.title: Subscripting
items.text: cbor_subscript_handler, modelled on jsonbsubs.c: - The subscript's type picks the meaning, just like ->: int, text, bytea or cbor. - Fetch behaves like ->. - Assignment creates missing levels like jsonb subscripting: a missing key step creates a map, a missing integer step creates an array padded with nulls; assigning past the end of an existing array pads it with nulls. A NULL column is treated as empty. Assigning below a scalar is an error, as is a NULL subscript. - Subscripts of type int2/int4/int8 index arrays or address integer map keys; bytea addresses byte-string keys; cbor addresses keys of any type; anything else (and untyped literals) is text.

Nested composites and arrays (nested arrays are dimensions) are converted; tags 0/1, 37 and 100 go to timestamptz, uuid and date columns. _valid (PostgreSQL 17+, as jsonb's) returns whether cbor_populate_record would succeed jsonb_to_record, _recordset cbor_to_record, … jsonb_strip_nulls(…, strip_in_arrays) cbor_strip_nulls(…, strip_in_arrays DEFAULT false, strip_undefined DEFAULT false) undefined is only stripped when strip_undefined is true jsonb_set, jsonb_set_lax, jsonb_insert cbor_set, cbor_set_lax, cbor_insert text[] path; typed-path versions are the *_path functions above jsonb_delete_path (#-) cbor_delete_text_path (#-) Renamed so it cannot be confused with the typed cbor_delete_path(cbor, cbor) jsonb_pretty cbor_pretty jsonb_typeof cbor_typeof Returns integer, float, bytes, text, array, map, tag, simple, boolean, null, undefined jsonb_path_* cbor_path_* Path queries, below

The set-returning functions run in value-per-call mode, using core iterators that borrow the detoasted datum. If pgrx 0.20 requires 'static iterators, the datum is copied once into the multi-call memory context.

populate_record value conversion, following jsonb's populate_record: - a text string goes through the column type's input function (also for array and composite columns) - an integer or float goes to numeric columns directly - bytes go to bytea - a map goes to a composite column; anything else but text is an error ("cannot call populate_composite on …"), and so is a top-level value that is not a map - an array goes to an array column: nested arrays are dimensions, taken from the first element at each level, and every sub-array must match them (at most 6); anything else but text is an error - anything else goes through its EDN text into the column's input function - a domain column converts to its base type, then checks the domain's constraints. Without a base row, an absent column is NULL and is checked too (NOT NULL domains fail); with one, absent columns keep the base row's values, and an empty map returns the base row - _valid makes every conversion and domain error a false result (soft errors; PostgreSQL 16 has no soft domain check, hence 17+). NULL for both arguments gives NULL, as jsonb's does

items.title: 9. Code architecture
items.text:
Cargo workspace, crates fetched from crates.io:

  • core/ (postcbor-core): pure Rust, no dependencies, #![forbid(unsafe_code)]. Every byte-level operation lives here.
  • cursor: the only code that indexes into input or body bytes. Every read is bounds-checked and returns Result.
  • normalize: input bytes → deterministic body, including unpacking (pack).
  • pack: unpacking packed input, and cbor_pack.
  • encode: shortest-form heads. float: float widths. bigint, num: bignums and decimal text for numeric.
  • datum: the stored form (header, body, index section); index: building and reading the index section, and rebasing it when extracting.
  • value: borrowed views (Value<'a>, which borrows its parsed Datum) and lazy iterators (ArrayIter<'a>, MapIter<'a>).
  • edn: parser and printer.
  • cmp: ordering, and the input to hashing.
  • ops: lookups, paths, containment and ? checks. edit: operations that build a new value (concatenation, deletion, set/insert, strip_nulls).
  • json: the decision logic for converting to and from JSON. Building and reading the actual jsonb values happens in the glue.
  • gin: the walk over a value's keys and atomic items, and the GIN entries built from it. jsonpath::gin: the entries and AND/OR program of a path query, and the path-equality form.
  • jsonpath: decoding PostgreSQL's compiled jsonpath (and a printer for tests), and the evaluator (jsonpath::eval), which calls a host trait for numeric arithmetic, input functions and regexes. decimal: exact decimals and jsonpath numbers, in and out of PostgreSQL's numeric binary form.
  • ctx, out, error: limits and interrupt checks, the output buffer trait, errors.
  • postcbor/: the pgrx cdylib. It holds the SQL definitions, the conversions to and from PostgreSQL types, the settings, and turning core errors into ereport calls. unsafe is allowed only where raw PostgreSQL APIs are unavoidable: datum (varlena wrapper, PallocBuf), io (receive buffer, encoding conversion), convert (to_cbor over any type: arrays, composites, catalog lookups), build (VARIADIC "any" and aggregate states), record (row construction), subscript, gin (GIN support functions), and path (the evaluator's host: numeric functions, input functions, regexes). Each unsafe block carries a one-line comment stating its invariant.
  • jsonb conversion goes through JSON text: cbor → jsonb prints JSON with the core's json module and calls jsonb_in; jsonb/json → cbor reads jsonb_out/json_out text with the EDN parser (JSON is a subset of EDN). Replace with direct JsonbValue building only if benchmarks show it matters.
  • fuzz/: cargo-fuzz targets. Depends only on postcbor-core. Not part of the default workspace build.

Core rules: - No powi/powf or other float functions without exact results: only basic IEEE operations and bit-level construction (float::pow2). Miri caught powi giving different results. - No recursion. Every walk keeps an explicit stack, limited by max_depth. One exception: the jsonpath evaluator recurses over the path expression, whose nesting is capped at 256 items when it is decoded (each recursion also checks PostgreSQL's stack limit). .**, the only step that descends by document depth, uses an explicit stack. - Checked arithmetic for every offset and length, and overflow-checks = true in the release profile. - Fallible allocation (try_reserve) for any buffer whose size comes from the input. The Rust allocator is malloc, and an allocation failure that isn't handled would abort the backend. - A declared length is never trusted for allocation. It is first checked against the bytes remaining. - Errors are Result<_, Error { kind, offset }>. A panic means a bug. - Limits and cancellation: operations that loop over input take a context (trait Ctx) carrying the limits and a check_interrupts() hook, called every 4096 items. The glue implements the hook with pgrx's check_for_interrupts!(). - Output goes straight into PostgreSQL memory. Every core function that produces bytes (datums, EDN, ->> text, bytea) writes through a buffer trait (OutBuf: reserve, append, patch a byte at a position, length). The core implements it for Vec<u8> for tests, Miri and fuzzing. - The glue's implementation (PallocBuf) allocates in the current memory context, with the 4-byte varlena header reserved at the front. It grows by doubling with repalloc, sets VARSIZE when finished, and returns the buffer as the datum, with no copy. - Start capacity: the input size when there is one (normalization, modifying functions), otherwise a small constant. - Aggregates write into a buffer allocated in the aggregate memory context. - Running out of memory in palloc/repalloc raises a PostgreSQL error. pgrx turns it into a panic, so Rust cleans up correctly, and the memory context frees the buffer.

items.title: 10. Testing
items.text:
• Core unit tests (cargo test -p postcbor-core): every normalization rule, every EDN form, format edge cases (index threshold boundaries, extraction rebasing).
  • Miri on postcbor-core tests.
  • Property tests, written as fuzz targets with arbitrary that generate valid values:
  • decode → encode → decode is the same value
  • EDN out → in is the same value
  • cmp is antisymmetric and transitive, and cmp = 0 ⟺ the bodies are equal, which implies equal hashes
  • an index lookup agrees with a linear scan
  • cbor_set followed by -> returns the value that was set
  • extracting a sub-value and re-normalizing it gives the same datum
  • normalizing any stored body again gives the same body (idempotence, section 6)
  • Byte-input fuzz targets: normalize (including packed input) and the EDN parser. The corpus is committed under fuzz/corpus/. Seeds: RFC 8949 Appendix A, regression cases, cbor2 output.
  • Cross-check against Python cbor2 (a test-only tool, uv run --with cbor2 tests/crosscheck.py [count]): random values encoded by cbor2 (plain and canonical) must be accepted, and their normalized form must decode to the same value, compared type-strictly (1 ≠ 1.0, -0.0 ≠ 0.0). It drives the core through core/examples/normalize_lines.rs.
  • SQL tests: pg_regress suites under postcbor/tests/pg_regress/, run by cargo pgrx regress against pgrx-managed PostgreSQL 15, 16, 17 and 18 (make test-matrix). make test runs them against the major of PG_CONFIG. Some suites have a second expected output (*_1.out) for PostgreSQL 15 and 16.
  • CI (GitHub Actions) runs clippy and the SQL suites on each version, Miri, and every fuzz target for 30 s, on each push and pull request.

items.title: Functions
items.text: Every jsonb_* function has a cbor_* counterpart that takes and returns cbor. Where this page says "as jsonb_x", the function behaves like its jsonb counterpart, described in PostgreSQL's JSON functions documentation, and only the differences are listed. Functions that exist only for CBOR are described in full below.

items.title: Building values
Taking values apart
items.text:
Function Differences from jsonb cbor_each(cbor) Returns (key cbor, value cbor): keys keep their type cbor_each_text(cbor) Returns (key text, value text), both converted with the ->> rules cbor_object_keys(cbor) Returns setof cbor, keeping each key's type cbor_array_elements(cbor) As jsonb_array_elements cbor_array_elements_text(cbor) As jsonb_array_elements_text, with the ->> rules cbor_array_length(cbor) As jsonb_array_length cbor_extract_path(cbor, VARIADIC text[]), _text As jsonb_extract_path, _text cbor_typeof(cbor) Returns one of integer, float, bytes, text, array, map, tag, simple, boolean, null, undefined

The ->> rules: a text string gives its text, null gives SQL NULL, anything else gives its EDN text.

items.text: cbor_get, cbor_get_text, cbor_get_path, cbor_get_path_text, cbor_has, cbor_has_any, cbor_has_all, cbor_delete and cbor_delete_path are the operators with keys of any type; see Operators.

items.title: Tags and simple values
items.text:
cbor_tag(cbor) → bigint The tag number, or NULL if the value is not tagged. An error if the number is above the largest bigint. cbor_untag(cbor) → cbor The tag's content, or the value itself if it is not tagged. cbor_tagged(tag bigint, value cbor) → cbor The value wrapped in a tag, then normalized, so cbor_tagged(2, 'h''01''') gives 1 (a bignum that fits in 64 bits). cbor_simple(n int) → cbor The simple value n, from 0–23 or 32–255. 20 to 23 give false, true, null and undefined; 24–31 are not valid simple values. cbor_undefined() → cbor undefined. 
SELECT cbor_tag('1(5)'), cbor_untag('1(5)'), cbor_tagged(32, '"https://example.com"'), cbor_simple(16);
-- 1 | 5 | 32("https://example.com") | simple(16)

items.title: Bytes and text
items.text: cbor_from_bytea(bytea) → cbor The same as bytea::cbor: decodes and normalizes CBOR bytes, unpacking packed CBOR. cbor_pack(value cbor, format text DEFAULT 'cbor-x') → bytea The value as packed CBOR, 'cbor-x' or 'ietf'. See Packed CBOR. cbor_diag(value cbor, pretty bool DEFAULT false) → text The EDN text, indented like cbor_pretty when pretty is true. cbor_byte_length(cbor) → bigint The length of the canonical encoding in bytes, as cbor::bytea would give it. cbor_to_jsonb_strict(cbor) → jsonb Like ::jsonb, but an error on anything JSON cannot represent exactly. See Casts.

items.title: How this was built
items.text:
postcbor was written entirely by Claude, Anthropic's AI model, working through Claude Code: the Rust code, the SQL definitions, the tests, the fuzz targets, the specification and this documentation.

A human set the goals and made the design decisions: what the type should do, how it compares to jsonb, and the architecture. The choice of Rust with pgrx rather than C was theirs, made for memory safety on untrusted input. They directed the work and reviewed it at the level of design and tests, not line by line. They are not a Rust developer.

So no human has read most of the code. What stands behind it is mechanical:

  • No unsafe code in the core. All parsing of user bytes happens in a crate that forbids unsafe and has no dependencies, so a parsing bug is a Rust error or panic (turned into an SQL error), not memory corruption. unsafe code exists only in the extension's calls to PostgreSQL's C interfaces.
  • Fuzzing. Fuzz targets feed arbitrary bytes and generated values to the parser, the EDN reader, packing, editing and jsonpath, and check properties such as "reading a value back gives the same value" and "the sort order agrees with equality".
  • Miri runs the core tests while checking for undefined behaviour.
  • SQL regression suites on PostgreSQL 15, 16, 17 and 18, including PostgreSQL's own jsonpath tests run on both jsonb and cbor.
  • Cross-checks against other implementations: Python's cbor2 and JavaScript's cbor-x.

All of these are run locally during development. A CI configuration runs clippy, the SQL suites, Miri and a short fuzzing pass on every change, but the repository is not yet published, so it has not run there yet; the cross-checks are run by hand.

Judge it accordingly. The tests cover what was thought of; review by someone who knows Rust and PostgreSQL internals would cover what was not. Reports of bugs, and especially of anything a crafted input can do to a server, are welcome.

items.title: btree and hash
items.text:
cbor has default btree and hash operator classes, so CREATE INDEX ON t (c), UNIQUE, ORDER BY, DISTINCT, GROUP BY and hash joins work as for any type. The btree order is described in Operators.

To index the value of one key, index an expression, as with jsonb:

CREATE INDEX ON events ((payload -> 'device'));

items.title: GIN
items.text:
Two GIN operator classes, as for jsonb:

CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (payload);                  -- cbor_ops, the default
CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (payload cbor_path_ops);    -- @> only; smaller and more selective
Class Operators Indexes cbor_ops (default) @>, ?, ?|, ?&, ?#, ?#|, ?#&, @?, @@ Each map key and each scalar, separately cbor_path_ops @> Each scalar together with the keys leading to it

cbor_ops can answer key existence because keys are indexed on their own; cbor_path_ops cannot, but its entries are more specific, so containment queries find fewer candidate rows. Both classes are lossy: every candidate row is checked again, so results are always exact.

Keys and values keep their CBOR type in the index: 1, "1" and 1.0 are different entries, just as @> treats them as different values. For path queries the index also holds each number in a single form, so @@ '$.n == 1' finds rows where n is 1, 1.0 or 4([0, 1]).

cbor_ops keeps array elements and map values apart, where jsonb_ops does not. A query such as @> '{"addr": {"zip": 5}}' therefore finds fewer false candidates than on jsonb when other rows have 5 inside an array.

items.title: Path queries
items.text:
With cbor_ops, @? and @@ use the index for conditions of the form accessors == literal (accessors being .key, .*, .**, […], [*] and filters on them), combined with &&, || and !, as jsonb_ops does. A path without such a condition scans the whole index. cbor_path_ops does not support path queries.

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @? '$.id ? (@ == 42)';
-- Bitmap Heap Scan on events
--   Recheck Cond: (payload @? '$."id"?(@ == 42)'::jsonpath)
--   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_payload_idx
--         Index Cond: (payload @? '$."id"?(@ == 42)'::jsonpath)

items.title: Queries that scan the whole index
items.text:
• @> with a value that has no scalars: {}, [], {"a": {}}.
  • ?# with a key that is an array or map, and ?#| when any of its keys is one.
  • @? and @@ without an == condition.

These still give the right result; they just do not benefit from the index.

items.title: Install
items.text: postcbor is built from source; there are no pre-built packages yet.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• PostgreSQL 15, 16, 17 or 18, with its server development files (Debian/Ubuntu: postgresql-server-dev-NN) and the headers they include (Debian/Ubuntu: libicu-dev).
  • Rust, at the version pinned in rust-toolchain.toml.
  • cargo-pgrx 0.20.0: cargo install cargo-pgrx --version 0.20.0 --locked.
  • clang, libclang and llvm from one LLVM release (Debian/Ubuntu: clang libclang-dev llvm), plus build-essential.

items.title: Build and install
items.text:
make PG_CONFIG=/path/to/pg_config
make install PG_CONFIG=/path/to/pg_config                              # as a user who can write PostgreSQL's directories
make install PG_CONFIG=/path/to/pg_config PGRX_INSTALL_FLAGS=--sudo    # or let it use sudo

PG_CONFIG selects the PostgreSQL installation; it defaults to the pg_config on your PATH. make registers that installation with pgrx in target/pgrx-home, so your ~/.pgrx is left alone. This sequence is tested from scratch on the postgres:18 Docker image.

Then, in each database:

CREATE EXTENSION postcbor;

items.title: UTF-8 databases only
items.text: CREATE EXTENSION postcbor fails in a database whose encoding is not UTF-8. CBOR text strings are UTF-8, and supporting other encodings would mean converting every text argument, path, column name and output at the boundary, for databases that are rare in practice.

items.title: Operators
items.text:
The operators are jsonb's, with the same symbols and meaning, plus ?#, ?#| and ?#& for keys of any type. Missing keys and out-of-range indexes give NULL, as in jsonb.

Operator Right side Result Meaning -> int cbor Array element (negative counts from the end), or integer key of a map -> text, bytea cbor Text key, byte-string key ->> same as -> text Same, as text (see below) #>, #>> text[] cbor, text Value at a text path @>, <@ cbor bool Contains, is contained in ? text bool Text key exists, or the top-level array has that text string ?|, ?& text[] bool Any of, all of the text keys exist ?# cbor bool Key of any type exists, or the top-level array has that element ?#|, ?#& cbor (an array of keys) bool Any of, all of the keys exist || cbor cbor Merge maps, concatenate arrays - text, text[], int, bytea cbor Delete a key, several text keys, or an array element #- text[] cbor Delete at a text path @?, @@ jsonpath bool Path query matches, path predicate holds =, <>, <, <=, >, >= cbor bool Equality and ordering

items.title: Reading values
items.text:
SELECT v -> 'a', v -> 1, v -> '\x01'::bytea, v #> '{a,b,1}', v ->> 1
FROM (SELECT '{"a": {"b": [10, 20]}, 1: "one", h''01'': "bytes"}'::cbor AS v) s;
-- {"b": [10, 20]} | "one" | "bytes" | 20 | one

An integer on the right reads an array element, or the integer key of a map, so cwt -> 1 reads key 1 of a CWT claims map.

->> and #>> give a text string as its text, null as SQL NULL, and anything else as its EDN text: '{"b": h''ff''}'::cbor ->> 'b' is h'ff'.

A path for #> (a text path) follows jsonb's rules: each step is a text key, or an array index when it reads as an integer and the value at that point is an array.

items.title: Keys of any type
items.text:
The operators only take text, integer and byte-string keys. For other keys (floats, tags, true, arrays…) and for paths whose steps keep their type (a typed path, written as a CBOR array), use the functions:

Function Like cbor_get(value, key cbor), cbor_get_text(value, key cbor) ->, ->> cbor_get_path(value, path cbor), cbor_get_path_text(value, path cbor) #>, #>> cbor_has(value, key cbor), cbor_has_any(value, keys cbor), cbor_has_all(value, keys cbor) ?#, ?#|, ?#& cbor_delete(value, key cbor), cbor_delete_path(value, path cbor) -, #- cbor_set_path, cbor_insert_path cbor_set, cbor_insert (see Functions) 
SELECT cbor_get(v, 'h''01'''), cbor_get_path(v, '["a", "b", 0]'), v ?# '1', v ? '1'
FROM (SELECT '{"a": {"b": [10, 20]}, 1: "one", h''01'': "bytes"}'::cbor AS v) s;
-- "bytes" | 10 | t | f

These are separate names, not overloads of -> and #>, because of how PostgreSQL types a quoted literal. With an operator taking cbor on the right, v -> 'a' would read 'a' as CBOR text (invalid EDN), and v -> '1' would quietly look up integer key 1 instead of text key "1".

The same applies to function overloads: cbor_delete(v, '1') reads '1' as text and deletes the text key "1". Write cbor_delete(v, '1'::cbor) to delete integer key 1.

items.title: Containment
items.text:
@> follows jsonb: a map contains another when it has each of its keys with a containing value; an array contains another when each element of the other is contained in some element, in any order; a scalar contains only itself. A tag contains a value with the same tag number whose content it contains. Decimal fractions and bigfloats (tags 4 and 5) are numbers, compared whole.

SELECT '{"a": 1, "tags": ["x", "y"]}'::cbor @> '{"tags": ["x"]}';
-- t

Containment is typed: '{"a": 1}'::cbor @> '{"a": 1.0}' is false, since 1 and 1.0 are different values.

items.title: Merging and deleting
items.text:
SELECT '{"a": 1}'::cbor || '{"b": 2}', '[1]'::cbor || '2', '{"a": 1, 1: 2}'::cbor - 1, '{"a": {"b": 1, "c": 2}}'::cbor #- '{a,b}';
-- {"a": 1, "b": 2} | [1, 2] | {"a": 1} | {"a": {"c": 2}}

|| follows jsonb: two maps merge (the right side wins on equal keys), and anything else is concatenated as arrays, a non-array side counting as a one-element array. On a map, - 1 deletes integer key 1; on an array it deletes element 1.

items.title: Subscripting
items.text:
value[…] reads like -> and can be assigned in UPDATE. The subscript's type picks the meaning: integers index arrays or address integer keys, bytea addresses byte-string keys, cbor addresses keys of any type, and anything else, including a quoted literal, is a text key.

CREATE TABLE t (c cbor);
INSERT INTO t VALUES ('{"a": [1]}');
UPDATE t SET c['a'][3] = '"x"';
UPDATE t SET c[1] = 'true';
SELECT c, c['a'][0] FROM t;
-- {1: true, "a": [1, null, null, "x"]} | 1

Assignment follows jsonb: missing levels are created (a map for a key, an array for an integer), and assigning past the end of an array pads it with nulls. A NULL column is treated as empty. Assigning below a scalar is an error, and so is a NULL subscript.

items.title: Equality and ordering
items.text:
Two values are equal when they are the same CBOR value: same types, same contents. 1 and 1.0 are not equal, and -0.0 is not equal to 0.0. Cast to numeric to compare numbers across types.

The sort order (used by ORDER BY, btree indexes and DISTINCT) first compares type, in this order:

  1. numbers: integers, floats and bignums, compared by exact value
  2. byte strings
  3. text strings
  4. arrays
  5. maps
  6. other tags
  7. simple values other than those below
  8. false
  9. true
  10. null
  11. undefined

Within a type:

  • Numbers compare by their exact mathematical value, so 1 < 1.5 < 2. NaN sorts after every other number. When an integer and a float are equal, the integer sorts first, and -0.0 sorts before 0.0.
  • Byte strings and text strings compare byte by byte, a prefix first. Text ignores the database collation and sorts by code point (its UTF-8 bytes), so an operating system collation upgrade cannot corrupt indexes.
  • Arrays compare element by element, a prefix first.
  • Maps with fewer entries sort first; then key 1, value 1, key 2, … in stored key order.
  • Tags compare by number, then by content. Simple values compare by number.

items.title: Path queries
items.text:
Path queries use PostgreSQL's own jsonpath language and type: the same paths you write for jsonb work on cbor.

cbor jsonb counterpart value @? path @?: does the path return any item? value @@ path @@: the result of a path predicate cbor_path_exists(target, path, vars DEFAULT '{}', silent DEFAULT false) jsonb_path_exists cbor_path_match(…) jsonb_path_match cbor_path_query(…) → setof cbor jsonb_path_query cbor_path_query_array(…) jsonb_path_query_array cbor_path_query_first(…) jsonb_path_query_first cbor_path_exists_tz, cbor_path_match_tz, cbor_path_query_tz, cbor_path_query_array_tz, cbor_path_query_first_tz the _tz variants, which allow datetime conversions that depend on the session time zone

vars is a cbor map whose text keys are the path's $variables.

SELECT v @? '$.items[*] ? (@.price > 5)', cbor_path_query_array(v, '$.items[*] ? (@.price > 5).id')
FROM (SELECT '{"items": [{"id": 1, "price": 2.5}, {"id": 2, "price": 10}]}'::cbor AS v) s;
-- t | [2]

SELECT cbor_path_exists('{"items": [{"id": 1}, {"id": 2}]}', '$.items[*] ? (@.id == $want)', '{"want": 2}');
-- t

For any value that converts to jsonb without loss, the results are those of the jsonb_path_* function on value::jsonb. A test suite runs PostgreSQL's own jsonpath tests on both types and compares the results; the only differences are the .keyvalue() ids described below.

items.title: CBOR types in paths
items.text:
jsonpath was designed for JSON. CBOR's extra types behave as follows:

  • Numbers compare by value inside paths, as in SQL/JSON: '1'::cbor @@ '$ == 1.0' is true, although '1'::cbor = '1.0' is false. Bignums, decimal fractions (tag 4) and bigfloats (tag 5) are numbers.
  • Arithmetic is decimal, as for jsonb, and its results have the same scale. A whole result is an integer; any other result is a decimal fraction (tag 4), so $.p * 2 with p = 2.5 gives 4([-1, 50]) (5.0). Items taken unchanged from the value keep their form: a float stays a float.
  • Byte strings have .type() "bytes". Two byte strings compare by their bytes; comparing one with another type is unknown, as for mismatched types in jsonpath.
  • Tags 0 and 1 (date and time) are datetimes, with .type() "timestamp with time zone", when their content is a valid date and time. Tags 2–5 are numbers when their content is valid. Other tags are transparent: the path sees their content, and an item returned from the value keeps its tag.
  • Map keys that are not text: .key only matches text keys. .* and .keyvalue() visit every entry, and .keyvalue() gives each key as its CBOR value.
  • undefined and simple values have their own types (.type() is "undefined" or "simple"), and are not equal to null.
  • NaN and infinities are numbers, ordered as numeric orders them.
SELECT cbor_path_query('{1: "a", "b": h''ff'', "t": 1(1700000000)}', '$.*.type()');
-- "string"
-- "bytes"
-- "timestamp with time zone"

.keyvalue() returns an id for each object, unique as in jsonb. The ids equal jsonb's for maps at the top of the value; for nested maps they differ, because jsonb derives them from its own storage layout.

items.title: PostgreSQL versions
items.text: The jsonpath methods added in PostgreSQL 17 (.bigint(), .boolean(), .date(), .decimal(), .integer(), .number(), .string(), .time(), .time_tz(), .timestamp(), .timestamp_tz()) are only available on PostgreSQL 17 and later, since the jsonpath type of earlier versions cannot express them.

items.title: Indexes
items.text: @? and @@ can use a GIN index with the default cbor_ops class, for conditions of the form accessors == literal, as jsonb_ops does. See Indexes.

items.title: Performance
items.text: Measured on 2026-11-18 (storage) and 2026-11-19 (timings) against jsonb: PostgreSQL 18, built without assertions for the timings, and a release build of postcbor, on one development machine. Ratios are cbor time divided by jsonb time, measured back to back (below 1 means cbor is faster). They are a rough guide, not a benchmark suite: run bench/lookup.sql on your own data and hardware before deciding.

items.title: Storage
items.text: Data cbor jsonb 200,000 small values ({"id", "name", "tags": [3 items], "active"}) 15 MB 27 MB 2,000 maps of 1,000 keys 16 MB 19 MB

items.title: Small values
items.text:
200,000 rows of the small values above, no index, best of 5 runs:

Query cbor / jsonb ->> 'name' 1.46 @> '{"active": true}' 1.65 @> '{"id": 5}' 1.30 ? 'name' 1.16 ? 'id' 1.04 text output 1.1 DISTINCT 0.87

Reading one key of a small map is slower than in jsonb: below 16 entries, cbor steps over the earlier entries one by one, where jsonb searches a table of offsets.

items.title: Large maps
items.text: Reading one key out of 1,000: ratio 0.8. Maps and arrays with 16 entries or more carry an index of their entries, so a lookup does not scan.

items.title: GIN indexes
items.text:
200,000 small values with a nested map:

  • Index sizes are the same as jsonb's: 29 MB for cbor_ops and jsonb_ops, 24 MB for cbor_path_ops and jsonb_path_ops. Index builds are 3–5% faster.
  • Indexed @> queries run within 10–20% of jsonb, with one exception in cbor's favour: @> '{"active": true, "addr": {"zip": 5}}' with the default class takes 1.9 ms against 10.1 ms, because cbor_ops keeps array elements and map values apart (see Indexes).

items.title: Path queries
items.text:
Without an index, on 200,000 small values, path operators are 2 to 4 times slower than jsonb's:

Query cbor jsonb @@ '$.id < 1000' 33 ms 10 ms @? '$.addr ? (@.city == "c1")' 37 ms 12 ms @? '$.** ? (@ == 1)' 256 ms 61 ms

Most of the gap is the cost of each function call rather than the path evaluation itself.

items.title: Settings and limits
items.text: postcbor treats every input as hostile: values arrive from applications over the network through ::cbor, bytea::cbor and the binary protocol. Every input path goes through the same checks and limits.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Setting Default Limits postcbor.max_depth 512 Nesting depth of a value. Each array, map and tag counts as one level postcbor.max_expansion_ratio 16 Size of a value after unpacking, divided by the size of its input postcbor.max_expanded_size 256MB Size of a value after unpacking

Only superusers can change them (SET, ALTER ROLE … SET, ALTER DATABASE … SET, or the server configuration).

The depth limit also applies to values built by functions and operators (||, cbor_set, cbor_build_array, subscript assignment, …): a value deeper than input accepts could be stored but not dumped and restored.

The expansion limits matter for packed CBOR, where a small input can unpack to a very large value. Raise postcbor.max_expansion_ratio for data that is legitimately packed more than 16 times.

Values are also limited by PostgreSQL's maximum of 1 GB per field.

items.title: Errors
Text form
items.text:
cbor values are written and shown in CBOR Extended Diagnostic Notation (EDN), the text form defined for CBOR. EDN is a superset of JSON, so any JSON text is a valid cbor literal.

SELECT '{"name": "ann", 1: h''cafe'', "when": 1(1700000000), "n": 2.5}'::cbor;
-- {1: h'cafe', "n": 2.5, "name": "ann", "when": 1(1700000000)}

Inside an SQL string literal, a single quote is doubled: the EDN h'cafe' is written h''cafe''.

items.title: Writing values
How values are shown
items.text:
Output is always written the same way: ", " between items and ": " after keys (as jsonb does), integers in decimal, floats in the shortest decimal that reads back as the same value (always with a . or an exponent, so 1.0 stays recognisably a float), bytes as lowercase h'…', and integers beyond 64 bits as 2(h'…') or 3(h'…').

cbor_pretty(value) and cbor_diag(value, pretty => true) indent with 4 spaces, one entry per line, like jsonb_pretty:

SELECT cbor_pretty('{"a": [1, 2], "b": {"c": h''ff''}}');
-- {
--     "a": [
--         1,
--         2
--     ],
--     "b": {
--         "c": h'ff'
--     }
-- }

items.title: One stored form
items.text:
Every value is stored in a single canonical form, whatever form it arrived in:

  • map keys are sorted by their encoded bytes: integers, byte strings, text strings, arrays, maps, tags, then floats and simple values, and within each type shorter keys first;
  • integers, lengths and tag numbers use their shortest encoding;
  • floats use the shortest of 16, 32 or 64 bits that holds the value exactly; every NaN becomes one NaN, and -0.0 stays distinct from 0.0;
  • indefinite-length arrays, maps and strings become definite;
  • bignums that fit in 64 bits become plain integers;
  • packed CBOR is unpacked.

So two values are equal exactly when they are the same CBOR value, and the output never depends on how the input was written:

SELECT '{"b": 1, "a": 2}'::cbor;
-- {"a": 2, "b": 1}

Input is rejected when a map has the same key twice (after normalization: {1: 0, 2(h'01'): 0} has key 1 twice), when a text string is not valid UTF-8, or when there is anything after the value. Other tags are kept as written; their content is only checked when an operation interprets them, for example a cast to timestamptz.

Byte strings are never looked into, including embedded CBOR (tag 24 or <<…>>): their bytes are kept as they are.
